extracted.intended_audience: federal judges, patent litigators, and trial practitioners (Northern District of California)
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for patent trials (Northern District of California) covering damages (lost profits, reasonable royalty), commencement of damages, and glossary definitions of patent-law terms. Intended to guide judges in instructing juries and to articulate legal standards to be applied at trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages attributable to infringing features / footprint in the marketplace
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee must seek only those damages attributable to the infringing features; lost profits must be tied to the intrinsic value of the patented feature; the trial court must carefully tie proof of damages to the claimed invention's footprint in the marketplace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: ResQNet.com, Calico Brand, Dow Chem., Integra, Grain Processing, Maxwell, Rite-Hite, Lam. Emphasizes that damages awards must be causally linked to the claimed invention and not to unrelated commercial success or advantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: No remote or speculative damages; proof with reasonable certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent holder is not entitled to damages that are remote or speculative. While a patent holder is not required to prove its damages with mathematical precision, it must prove them with reasonable certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: remote consequences (e.g., heart attack of the inventor, loss in stock value) are not compensable. Authority: Lucent, Lam, Standard Havens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubts about amount of damages resolved against alleged infringer (when due to infringer's records failure)
rubrics_metrics.description: When amount of damages cannot be ascertained with precision, any doubts regarding the amount must be resolved against the alleged infringer. Adverse consequences must rest on the alleged infringer when inability to ascertain lost profits is due to the infringer's failure to keep accurate records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: Lam. Applies when the infringer's own recordkeeping prevents precise calculation of patentee's damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit 'but for' test for lost profits (four elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: To recover lost profits, the patent holder must show a causal relationship between the infringement and its loss of profit — i.e., but for the infringement there is a reasonable probability the patentee would have earned higher profits. The four Panduit elements are: (1) demand for the patented product/method; (2) no acceptable noninfringing substitutes (or allocation of market share despite substitutes); (3) manufacturing and marketing capacity to make the sales; and (4) the amount of profit the patentee would have made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The four-factor Panduit test (Panduit Corp. v. Stahlin Bros.) has been adopted by the Federal Circuit but is not the only method. Once patentee establishes the four elements, burden shifts to alleged infringer to show the but-for analysis is unreasonable. Authorities: Panduit, Rite-Hite, BIC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — demand
rubrics_metrics.description: Demand for the patented product can be proven by significant sales of the patentee's patented product or significant sales of an infringing product containing the patented features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: DePuy Spine v. Medtronic Sofamor Danek. Use either patentee's sales or infringer's sales showing market demand for the patented features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — noninfringing substitutes: acceptability
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'acceptable' noninfringing substitute must have the advantages of the patented invention that were important to purchasers of the alleged infringer's product. If purchasers were motivated by features available only from the infringing product and the patentee's product, other alternatives are not acceptable substitutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If market realities show competitors would likely have captured the sales despite product differences, patentee is not entitled to lost profits. Authorities: Am. Seating, Standard Havens, SmithKline Diagnostics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — noninfringing substitutes: availability
rubrics_metrics.description: An alternative product may be considered 'available' even if it was not actually on sale during the infringement period if the material, experience, and know-how for the substitute were readily available. Factors against availability include prohibitively high cost or need to design/invent around the patented technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of readiness of materials/know-how supports availability; lack of equipment/know-how at time of infringement suggests unavailability. Authorities: Grain Processing, Micro Chem. v. Lextron.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentee is entitled to lost profits only for sales it could have actually made. Patentee must show it is more probable than not that it could have made and sold, or had someone else make or sell for it, the additional products it says it would have sold but for the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof may include evidence of ability to expand manufacturing/marketing to meet increased demand. Authority: Fonar; Gyromat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — amount of profit (calculation method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lost profits on lost sales may be calculated by computing the lost revenue for sales patentee claims it would have made but for the infringement and subtracting additional costs/expenses it would have incurred in making those lost sales (e.g., cost of goods, sales costs, packaging, shipping). Fixed costs that do not vary with production (taxes, insurance, rent, administrative overhead) should not be subtracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: Paper Converting Mach. Co. v. Magna-Graphics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — market share method
rubrics_metrics.description: If patentee establishes it would have made some, but not all, of the infringer's sales, the lost sales amount may be shown by proving the patentee's share of the relevant market (excluding infringing products). Market share award may be made even if noninfringing substitutes were available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining market requires identifying which products are in that market: products are in same market if 'sufficiently similar' — not significantly higher priced nor possessing significantly different characteristics. Authorities: State Indus., BIC, Micro Chem., Crystal Semiconductor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — collateral sales
rubrics_metrics.description: To recover lost profits on collateral products (products sold along with the competitive product), patentee must prove (1) it is more likely than not that it would have sold the collateral products but for the infringement, and (2) the collateral product and the competitive product together are analogous to components of a single assembly or parts of a complete machine (i.e., a single functional unit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not recover lost profits for items that have no functional relationship and were sold only as a matter of convenience or business advantage. Authorities: Rite-Hite (denying recovery where nonpatented product lacked functional relationship); State Indus., Panduit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — price erosion
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentee can recover price-erosion damages if it proves that but for the infringement it would have been able to charge higher prices for some products. Damages equal the difference between (A) profits the patentee would have made at the higher price and (B) profits actually made at the lower price. Patentee must account for any drop in sales that would have resulted from charging a higher price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May also award increases in costs (e.g., additional marketing) caused by competition from the infringing product. Case law: compare Crystal Semiconductor (denial where patentee failed to show how higher prices would affect demand) with Ericsson (upholding award where market inelastic). See Vulcan Eng'g, Minco, BIC, Kalman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — entitlement
rubrics_metrics.description: If patentee has established infringement, it is entitled to at least a reasonable royalty to compensate for that infringement. If patentee fails to prove lost profits for some or all infringing sales, the court must award a reasonable royalty for those sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: 35 U.S.C. § 284; Lucent; Crystal Semiconductor; Fromson; Minco; Mahurkar; Rite-Hite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — definition (hypothetical negotiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty is the payment amount the patentee and alleged infringer would have agreed to in a hypothetical negotiation taking place before the infringement began. In that hypothetical negotiation assume both parties believed the patent was valid and infringed and both were willing to enter into a reasonable agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on expectations at negotiation time; evidence of events after the infringement may be considered only to the extent it aids assessment of the hypothetical negotiation. Although actual infringer profits may inform anticipated profits, royalty cannot be limited or increased based on actual profits. Authorities: Uniloc (25% rule inadmissible), ResQNet (licenses must be related to patent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty — relevant factors (Georgia-Pacific list and limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining a reasonable royalty, consider all facts known and available to the parties when infringement began. Typical factors (the Georgia-Pacific factors) include: (1) royalties previously received by patentee on the patent; (2) rates paid for comparable patents; (3) nature/scope of license (exclusive/nonexclusive); (4) licensor's policy to maintain monopoly; (5) commercial relationship between parties; (6) effect of patented specialty on sales of other products; (7) duration of patent/license; (8) established profitability/commercial success/popularity; (9) utility/advantages over prior modes; (10) nature/character of commercial embodiment; (11) extent of infringer's use; (12) customary portion of selling price/profit for use of invention; (13) portion of profit attributable to the invention vs other factors; (14) expert opinion/testimony; (15) the amount parties would have agreed upon in hypothetical negotiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Georgia-Pacific factors are admissible but not mandatory; instruct jury only on factors relevant to the evidence. If a Standard Essential Patent (SEP) or RAND obligation is involved, instruct jury to separate the value of the patented invention from added value due to standardization — do not consider the success of the standard itself. Authorities: Georgia-Pacific, Energy Transp. Group (Federal Circuit caution), Ericsson v. D-Link (erroneous instruction when irrelevant factors given), Uniloc, ResQNet, Lucent, others.

rubrics_metrics.name: SEP (Standard Essential Patent) valuation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the asserted patent is essential to an industry standard, the jury must ensure the damages award reflects only the value of the patented invention and not additional value resulting from inclusion in the standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury must differentiate between (a) added benefit of the technological invention and (b) added value arising from standardization; SEP holders should be compensated only for the added benefit of their inventions. Authority: Ericsson v. D-Link.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date of commencement of damages — products: marking and notice rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages commence on the date the alleged infringer has both infringed and been notified of the alleged infringement. If patentee sells a product that includes the claimed invention, determine whether the patentee has 'marked' the product with the patent number (placing 'patent' or 'pat.' with the number on substantially all products). Patentee bears burden of proving substantial compliance with marking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If patentee substantially complied with marking (including reasonable efforts by licensees), constructive notice applies and damages begin without actual notice. If not marked, damages begin on date alleged infringer received actual notice (filing of the complaint qualifies). If patent granted after infringing activity began, damages calculated from patent issue date; if patent granted before infringing activity began, from date infringement began. Authorities: 35 U.S.C. § 287; Crystal Semiconductor; Maxwell; Nike; Am. Med. Sys.; Devices for Med.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date of commencement of damages — method claims exception
rubrics_metrics.description: For method (process) claims, there is no marking/notice requirement. Calculation of damages for infringement of method claims begins as of the date the patent issued or the date the infringement began, whichever was first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: 35 U.S.C. § 287(c)(2)(F); Am. Med. Sys.; Crystal Semiconductor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract (glossary definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract: A brief summary of the technical disclosure in a patent to enable the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office and the public to determine quickly the nature and gist of the technical disclosure in the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment (glossary definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendment: A patent applicant’s change to one or more claims or to the specification either in response to an office action taken by an Examiner or independently by the patent applicant during the patent application examination process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (glossary definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipation: A situation in which a claimed invention describes an earlier invention and, therefore, is not considered new and is not entitled to be patented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment (glossary definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignment: A transfer of patent rights to another called an 'assignee' who, upon transfer, becomes the owner of the rights assigned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim (glossary definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim: Each claim of a patent is a concise, formal definition of an invention and appears at the end of the specification in a separately numbered paragraph. A claim marks the boundaries of the patent; claims may be independent or dependent (dependent claims refer to and incorporate other claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A device or method infringes only if it contains each and every requirement (limitation) of a claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conception (glossary definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception: The complete mental part of the inventive act which must be capable of proof, as by drawings, disclosure to another, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings (glossary definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings: Visual representations of the claimed invention contained in a patent application and issued patent, usually including several figures illustrating various aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements / Limitations / Requirement (glossary definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements / Limitation / Requirement: The required parts of a device or the required steps of a method. A limitation/requirement is a required part of an invention set forth in a patent claim and is often used interchangeably with the word 'requirement.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A device or method infringes a patent if it contains each and every requirement (limitation) of a patent claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embodiment (glossary definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Embodiment: A product or method that contains the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement (glossary definition / legal standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement: A description of the invention that is sufficient to enable persons skilled in the field of the invention to make and use the invention. The specification must contain such an enabling description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement is a statutory requirement for patent validity; instructions elsewhere control how jurors should apply the term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination (glossary definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examination: Procedure before the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office whereby an Examiner reviews the filed patent application to determine if the claimed invention is patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing Date (glossary definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing Date: Date a patent application, with all the required sections, has been submitted to the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement (glossary definition / standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement: Violation of a patent occurring when someone makes, uses, or sells a patented invention, without permission of the patent holder, within the United States during the term of the patent. Infringement may be direct, by inducement, or contributory. Direct infringement is making, using, or selling the patented invention without permission. Inducing infringement is intentionally causing another to directly infringe. Contributory infringement is offering to sell or selling an item that is a significant part of the invention so the buyer directly infringes; contributory infringer must know the part is designed specifically for infringing and not a common object suitable for noninfringing uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonobviousness (glossary definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonobviousness: One of the requirements for securing a patent. To be valid, the subject matter must not have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the field at the time of the earlier of the filing date or the date of invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office Action (glossary definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Office Action: A written communication from the Examiner to the patent applicant in the course of the application examination process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent (glossary definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent: An exclusive right granted by the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office to an inventor to prevent others from making, using, or selling an invention for a term of 20 years from the date the patent application was filed (or 17 years from issuance). The patent has three parts: specification, drawings, and claims; it is granted after examination (prosecution history).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent and Trademark Office (PTO) (glossary definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent and Trademark Office (PTO): An administrative branch of the U.S. Department of Commerce charged with overseeing and implementing federal patent and trademark laws; responsible for examining patent applications and issuing patents in the U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art (glossary definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior Art: Previously known subject matter in the field of a claimed invention for which a patent is sought. Includes issued patents, publications, and publicly available knowledge such as trade skills and practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution History (glossary definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution History: The complete written record of proceedings in the PTO from the initial application to the issued patent, including office actions and amendments filed during examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reads On (glossary definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reads On: A patent claim 'reads on' a device or method when each required part (requirement) of the claim is found in the device or method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to Practice (glossary definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduction to Practice: The invention is 'reduced to practice' when it is sufficiently developed to show it would work for its intended purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty (glossary definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Royalty: A payment made to the owner of a patent by a nonowner in exchange for rights to make, use, or sell the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification (glossary definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification: A required part of a patent application and an issued patent. It is a written description of the invention and of the manner and process of making and using the claimed invention.
